title: Scope, competence and site authority
audience: Supervisors, coordinators and trained cleaners who may be asked to triage, refer or document mould-related work in homes, rentals and commercial buildings, under an approved plan. Not a qualification or authority to remediate, demolish, or certify any building or room.
learningOutcomes: Identify who holds authority for the work and refuse work outside the contract or work order.
Separate observed, uncertain and unverified information in a written record.
Refer any scope mismatch before work continues.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson is training content. It does not authorise remediation, demolition, disturbance of building materials, handling of contaminated water or waste, or any statement that a space is safe or free of mould. Completing it gives no licence, certificate or approval. Restricted remediation is carried out only by a competent, appropriately qualified professional under an approved plan.

instruction.heading: Who decides before work starts
instruction.body: Before any practical work, confirm the contract boundary in writing, the responsible remediation manager, the access permission for the property, and the competence of each worker. Where the contract covers only routine cleaning, that is the limit of the task. The WA Department of Health guideline describes three duties that bear on mould: a general public health duty for anyone whose actions could foreseeably cause harm, a workplace duty, and a residential tenancies duty under which owners or agents must keep rental premises habitable and occupants help manage water, heating, ventilation and appliances. Which duty applies to a job depends on who controls the premises and the work. The coordinator confirms that position before work starts.

instruction.heading: Recognising a scope mismatch
instruction.body: A tenant who asks a cleaner to treat a damp bedroom after a long leak is asking for remediation, which the work order may not cover. The cleaner does not have authority to treat the room. Establish who may decide, what information is missing and which actions must stop. The absence of visible growth does not mean there is no hidden damage, so it cannot be used to widen the scope. A cleaning certificate also does not establish remediation competence for a particular job.

procedure: Stop before any practical work. Confirm the contract boundary in writing.
Identify the responsible remediation manager and who can authorise access.
Confirm each worker's competence and the protective arrangements for the job.
Write down what has been observed and what is still uncertain.
If the request goes beyond the work order, record it and refer it for a revised scope.
Restart only when the competent person has confirmed the scope in writing.

workedExamples.situation: A tenant asks a cleaner to treat a damp bedroom after a long leak. The agreed work order covers only routine cleaning.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Who may decide, what is missing and what must stop?
workedExamples.reasoning: The cleaner cannot decide. The work order does not cover treatment, and the leak source is unknown. Stop, record the request, and refer it to the responsible remediation manager for a revised scope and a competent assessment.

workedExamples.situation: A worker says the job is just cleaning, so no supervisor is needed, although the walls show visible mould.
workedExamples.reasoning: Not on the facts given. The WA guideline classes contamination as simple or complex, and the class decides whether professional help is needed. Only a competent assessment can make that call, so the worker stops until it has been made.

equipmentAndPpe: Written work order or contract boundary, with the access permission attached.
Competence record for each worker, confirmed by the responsible manager.
Training-only scenario cards. No real property, mould or contaminated material is handled in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Treating a damp room as routine cleaning because the occupant asked.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the work order. Routine cleaning does not include remediation. Refer for a revised scope.

commonErrors.error: Assuming no visible growth means there is no hidden damage.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the warning signs and refer concealed damage for competent investigation.

commonErrors.error: Accepting a general cleaning certificate as proof of remediation competence.
commonErrors.prevention: Require project-specific competence confirmed by the responsible manager.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not grant authority to remediate, demolish or disturb building materials, handle contaminated water or waste, or certify any area as safe. Completing it does not give a licence, certificate or approval.

Asbestos and lead disturbance, sewage remediation and certain waste handling are restricted to competent and, where the law requires, licensed people. The rules for each state and territory were not checked for this lesson.

qualityStandard: The learner identifies who holds authority for the work and refuses work outside the work order.
The learner writes the observed, uncertain and unverified items separately.
The learner refers any scope mismatch before work continues.
documentationEvidence: Written contract boundary and the access permission.
Record of the responsible remediation manager and each worker's confirmed competence.
Scope-mismatch record with the referral and the decision.
summary: The work order sets the limit of the task.
Authority to decide is named before work starts.
Visible growth and hidden damage are both recorded, and neither widens the scope alone.
A stop-and-refer decision is a valid outcome.

knowledgeChecks.question: A tenant asks a cleaner to treat a damp bedroom. The work order covers only routine cleaning. What is correct?
options: Treat the room, because the tenant asked.
Stop, record the request and refer it for a revised scope and competent assessment.
Treat only the visible mould and leave the rest.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about the duties in the WA guideline is correct?
options: Only the owner has any duty under the guideline.
The guideline gives every cleaner a licence to remediate.
The guideline sets out general public health, workplace and residential tenancy duties, and which applies depends on who controls the premises and the work.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker says a job is routine cleaning, so no supervisor is needed. What should happen?
options: The worker stops until the scope and contamination level have been assessed by a competent person.
The worker starts, because cleaners do not need supervision.
The worker starts and reports afterwards.

officialReferences.title: Guidelines for managing mould and dampness: related public health risks in buildings (WA Department of Health)
officialReferences.pageDate: April 2024 (version control table); publication code ENV-0014702 MAY'24; no separate last-updated date shown
officialReferences.covers: Read through a page-summary tool on 2026-11-03 (PDF, Environmental Health Directorate, WA Department of Health). Section 1.4 sets out a general public health duty, a workplace duty and a residential tenancies duty. Section 2.1 names people with existing respiratory, immunocompromising and allergic conditions, and infants, children and older people. Section 3.2.2 says porous items are often not economically salvageable and must be thrown out. Section 3.3 says the source must be located to address the cause and prevent recurrence. Section 3.4.1 defines simple contamination as new, isolated and visible, no greater than one square metre, with easily identified causes, and its footnote calls the one-square-metre size arbitrary. Section 3.4.2 defines complex contamination as larger than one square metre or found in multiple rooms or places. Section 3.5 states there are no defined quantitative or qualitative exposure thresholds for mould or dampness. Section 4.1 lists containment, drying and source repair as principles. Section 4.2.2 advises scrubbing hard surfaces with soapy water, avoiding dry brushing, cleaning at least 30 to 50 cm beyond the visible mould, removing or discarding porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned, stating that mould is not considered hazardous waste, and not painting, sealing or covering surfaces until dry. Section 4.3 recommends a site-specific plan with professionals for complex contamination, isolation with heavy grade plastic and negative pressure, and evacuation of occupants. Section 4.4 lists no recurrence within two to four weeks after remediation as an indicator of success, recommends the evaluation be done by a different entity, and states there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment. Appendix B recommends a P2 or N95 respirator and says PAPRs should be used for complex remediation. Appendix E says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to remediate, demolish, disturb building materials, handle contaminated water or waste, or certify that a building, room or occupant area is safe or free of mould or pathogens. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Restricted or high-exposure remediation is carried out only by an appropriately qualified and competent professional under an approved plan, and some related work, including asbestos and lead disturbance and certain waste handling, is restricted to licensed or specially authorised people. The owner, manager, tenant or contract may define what work is permitted, but where the contract covers only routine cleaning, that is the limit of the task. Where the controlling authority or the competent supervisor is not identified, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: the hazards are unknown or changing; the work is destructive or hazardous and outside the authorised scope; exposure is uncontrolled or the building is unsafe to occupy; supervision, equipment or permissions are insufficient; flood, sewage, asbestos or lead may be present; a worker's PPE or respirator readiness has not been verified; a client asks for a clearance or pathogen-free statement; or a waste route is unauthorised. A stop-work decision is correct. Record it and restart only after the competent supervisor has confirmed the scope in writing.
